title: Balancing Fairness and Accuracy in Credit Scoring: A Study on Performative Prediction and Disparate Impact
authors: Gentyala, R.; Mantravadi, S.; Jha, P.
tldr: An extensive experimental study on performative prediction in credit scoring demonstrates that fairness mitigation methods can harm demographic groups they aim to protect, proposing fairness-without-accuracy-loss regularization to improve fairness across all sensitive attributes simultaneously.
approach: Investigated four performative prediction techniques: repulsion field, performative log-loss, performative gradient step, and fair performative log-loss.
Conducted ablation study varying regularization strength, sensitive attribute, and fairness mitigation across 8+ datasets.
Introduced fairness-without-accuracy-loss regularization combining fairness and loss regularization to improve fairness while maintaining performance.
Applied stratified 5-fold cross-validation across multiple sensitive attributes (race, sex, age, marital status).
Evaluated using F1-Score, Demographic Parity, Equality of Opportunity, Equalized Odds, and Generalized Entropy Index.
Tested on datasets spanning healthcare, finance, criminal justice, and consumer domains to demonstrate generalizability.
Employed correlation analysis using Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, and Cramer's V to examine fairness-accuracy trade-offs.
Used SHAP analysis to explain model fairness and investigate how feature importance shifts with regularization.
findings: Fairness mitigation methods can paradoxically harm the demographic groups they are designed to help.
Intersectional fairness analysis (combinations of sensitive attributes) reveals unfairness invisible to single-attribute analysis.
Fairness-without-accuracy-loss regularization improves fairness across all sensitive attributes without degrading performance.
SHAP analysis reveals that fairness techniques do not alter feature importance of protected attributes.
The relationship between fairness and accuracy varies across datasets, sensitive attributes, and regularization strength.
Repulsion field performs best for fairness improvement but degrades accuracy more than other techniques.
Age and marital status can be strong predictors of credit outcomes, and mitigating them can improve fairness for related sensitive attributes.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides the first comprehensive experimental study of performative prediction effects on fairness in credit scoring, demonstrating that fairness mitigation methods can paradoxically harm the groups they aim to protect when performative feedback loops are ignored. It proposes fairness-without-accuracy-loss regularization that improves fairness across all sensitive attributes simultaneously, validates findings across eight heterogeneous datasets, and uses intersectional fairness analysis to reveal biases invisible under single-attribute analysis.
directly_justifies: Fairness mitigation methods can harm minority groups they are designed to protect under performative conditions.
Intersectional fairness analysis reveals biases invisible to single-attribute fairness metrics.
Fairness-without-accuracy-loss regularization improves fairness without sacrificing predictive performance.
SHAP analysis confirms fairness techniques do not alter the importance of protected features.
Age and marital status fairness can indirectly improve fairness for related sensitive attributes like race and sex.
limits: Evaluation limited to tabular datasets; results may differ for non-tabular or unstructured financial data.
Synthetic datasets used alongside real ones; generalization to purely real-world credit data requires further study.
Fairness metrics used (Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds) do not capture all dimensions of fairness.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: The paper was systematically scanned across all 14 topic domains. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) received high relevance as the core study is on credit scoring models, fairness metrics, regularization, and interpretability. Domain 5 (Behavioral Profiles) received medium relevance through demographic profile analysis. Domain 10 (Privacy) received low relevance for mentioning sensitive attributes. Domain 11 (User Correction) received medium relevance for addressing performative prediction's ability to correct biases in deployment. Domains 1-4, 7-9, 12-14 were considered and rejected as the paper does not address Filipino demographics, existing PFMS systems, budgeting, savings, anomaly detection, engagement, mobile design, or synthetic data generation.

limitations: Tabular-only evaluation; non-tabular data types not assessed.
Fairness metrics do not capture all fairness dimensions (e.g., individual fairness).
Performative prediction techniques require multiple training iterations increasing computational cost.
Intersectional analysis limited to pairwise combinations of sensitive attributes.

problem_and_motivation: Algorithms trained without performative considerations can reinforce and amplify existing biases. When fairness mitigation is applied without accounting for performative effects, it can harm minority groups it is intended to help. Standard fairness metrics focus on individual sensitive attributes in isolation, ignoring overlapping identities and shifting distributions after deployment.
